extracted.intended_audience: advertisers, PR professionals, regulators, environmental campaigners, and consumers interested in greenwashing/advertising standards
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether environmental claims in advertising (especially from high-carbon sectors) are misleading, sufficiently substantiated, and presented in a way consumers will correctly interpret. Focuses on distinctions between aspirational targets and present mitigating actions, required evidence, and the role of imagery/wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying current 'significant mitigating steps' unless true
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers would view the ad as a claim that Lufthansa had already taken “significant mitigating steps” to ensure that the net environmental impact of its business was not harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not create wording or imagery that gives the impression the advertiser has already implemented major mitigation measures. If only plans or intentions exist, make that explicit and avoid language that suggests present, completed action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present future aspirations as present achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: Lufthansa told the ASA that its environmental claims were based on aspirations, including becoming carbon neutral by 2050 and halving carbon emissions by 2030.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish clearly between aspirational targets/commitments and current performance. Claims based on distant targets can be misleading if consumers interpret them as current facts; ads should state timeframes and the provisional nature of commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute green claims require current, demonstrable support
rubrics_metrics.description: We also understood that there were currently no environmental initiatives or commercially viable technologies in the aviation industry which would substantiate the absolute green claim ‘protecting its future’, as we considered consumers would interpret it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid absolute language such as 'protecting the future' or 'CO2-neutral' unless there is present, verifiable evidence (e.g., commercially deployed technologies or operational initiatives) to support that absolute claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate environmental claims with robust evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers ... shouldn’t make claims that give consumers a misleading impression about their green credentials and plans or which they can’t substantiate with robust evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, robust, and preferably independent evidence for environmental claims. General statements, vague initiatives, or unsupported assertions are insufficient. Evidence should match how consumers are likely to interpret the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider consumer interpretation when judging misleadingness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASA said consumers would view the ad as a claim that Lufthansa had already taken 'significant mitigating steps' ... we considered consumers would interpret it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate ads from the perspective of an average consumer: what impression will they reasonably take away? If ordinary consumers are likely to infer more than the evidence supports, the ad may be misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in high-carbon sectors — higher scrutiny expected
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers in high carbon emitting sectors shouldn't make claims that give consumers a misleading impression about their green credentials and plans ... which they can't substantiate with robust evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies in industries with large environmental impacts (e.g., aviation, oil & gas, automotive) should apply stricter caution: avoid implying sector-level solutions exist when they do not, and ensure stronger substantiation and clearer qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imagery and straplines that overstate environmental performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The advert featured a picture of a plane overlaid on an image of the Earth and boasted the strap line #MakeChangeFly. 'Connecting the world. Protecting its future,' the poster read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visuals and short slogans can create strong, immediate impressions. Ensure imagery and straplines do not convey unsubstantiated or absolute environmental benefits; if imagery could imply more than text substantiates, revise visuals or add clarifying qualifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: When banned/misleading, remedy by clearer and better-substantiated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASA banned the ad campaign, telling Lufthansa to make clearer and better substantiated environmental claims in the future and to not give a misleading impression of the impact caused by flying with the airline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is found misleading, corrective action should include rewording to clarify status (e.g., 'we aim to... by [year]') and providing accessible substantiation. Avoid repeating the same unqualified claims without new evidence.
